transcript.text: My fridge freezer has been making a funny smell in the kitchen the last couple of days, I've cleaned it out but it's still there. Any ideas?

Yes, a few. When a smell survives a good clean, it's usually coming from somewhere the clean doesn't reach. The main thing that tells the causes apart is what the smell is like. If it's musty, sour or rotten-food:
1. Defrost drain hole: look on the back wall of the fridge section, low down, for a small channel and hole. Food bits and slime collect there and smell. Clear it gently with a cotton bud or pipe cleaner, then flush with a little warm water and bicarbonate of soda. If the water pools instead of draining, the drain is blocked, and that is very often the culprit.
2. Drip tray: unplug it first. Pull it out carefully and look at the back near the bottom, by the compressor. There's usually a small tray that the drain empties into. Stagnant water there can smell strongly. Empty and wash it if you can reach it.
3. Door seals: fold back the rubber gaskets and wipe inside the pleats with warm soapy water. Mould hides there.
4. Ice maker or water filter, if yours has one: an old filter or a stale ice bin can give a musty taste and smell.
5. Check it's still keeping cold. If it's warmer than usual, food will spoil quickly and that is a separate fault. If it's hot plastic, burning or fishy-electrical, especially from the back or the plug, switch it off at the socket and unplug it. Don't keep using it. That points to an electrical fault, which needs an engineer. So which is it, musty or rotten, or burning or chemical? And is it still cold as normal?
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.
It's more like hot plastic, an electrical sort of smell, not rotten food. It's stronger round the back of the fridge than inside it. The fridge and freezer are still cold as normal.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. Because it's still cooling normally, the fault is probably in a part that's struggling or overheating rather than one that has failed outright. 1. The compressor start relay or overload. This is a small plastic box clipped to the side of the compressor (the black, dome-shaped unit at the bottom of the back). These commonly overheat and scorch while the fridge still seems to work.
2. A wiring connector or a fan motor at the back. Some models have a small fan by the compressor, and a loose or corroded connection or a struggling motor can cook its plastic.
3. The plug, mains lead or socket. A loose pin or a poor connection in the socket can get hot enough to smell. 1. Look at the plug and the wall socket for browning, melted plastic or a hot spot. Marks there point to the plug, lead or socket. Don't plug anything else into that socket until it's been looked at.
2. With a torch, look at the back near the bottom without removing any covers. Look for discoloured or melted plastic, especially on the small box on the side of the compressor, or for a scorched cable. Marks there point to the relay or the wiring.
3. Think about whether it has tripped the electrics or blown a fuse recently. That would suggest an electrical fault rather than just overheating. Whatever you find, the fix is for an engineer: this is mains wiring and parts on the compressor. In the meantime, keep the freezer door shut. A full freezer usually stays frozen for about a day. If the engineer can't come quickly, move the most important food to a cool box or a neighbour's freezer. On repair versus replacement: if it turns out to be the start relay, a connector or the plug, that's usually an inexpensive repair. It's only worth thinking about replacement if the engineer finds the compressor itself is at fault on an older fridge freezer. Can you see any scorching on the plug, socket or at the back, and has it tripped the electrics at all?

The plug feels a bit warm when I touch it, but the socket looks ok. No smoke and the fuse box hasn't tripped. I can't pull the fridge out to look at the back myself, it's too heavy. There's also an occasional buzzing from the back. Should I unplug it?

Yes, unplug it now and leave it off. A hot-plastic smell from the back together with a warm plug means something electrical is getting hotter than it should. A plug should feel at room temperature, not warm. It isn't safe to keep running it while you wait for an engineer. 1. The compressor start relay or overload. This is the small plastic box on the side of the compressor. A relay that's failing often buzzes or chatters as it tries to start the compressor and cooks its own plastic.
2. A poor connection in the plug or mains lead. A loose terminal or a fuse that isn't seated well makes heat right at the plug. That could explain the warmth even though the socket looks fine.
3. Less likely, a connector or small fan motor at the back overheating. 1. Look closely at the plug pins and the plug body, and run your fingers along the first part of the lead. Browning on the pins, a soft or misshapen spot, or a lead that feels warmer near the plug points to the plug or lead. A clean, cool plug points back to the relay at the compressor. Some buzzing on its own can be normal. A click and then a steady hum as the compressor starts is what fridges do all day. A click-buzz-click every few minutes is a common sign of a struggling relay. Since you can't pull it out, and the likely part sits on the compressor, this is one for an engineer. They can move it safely and check the relay, the wiring and the plug. It's usually a modest repair if it's the relay or a connection. Don't use that socket for anything else until you're sure the socket isn't involved.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.

Electrical overheating (hot plastic or burning smell from the back) (low)
